<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-organized cases, but PRO's core claim survived the exchange better: the motion asks a comparative question ("more like banks/MMFs than like software"), and PRO consistently showed that any workable stablecoin regime—reserve verification, enforceable liquidity floors calibrated to redemption stress, supervisory examination, redemption priority—is self-evidently much closer to bank/MMF-style prudential financial regulation than to ordinary software governance, without needing to import every single bank tool (capital ratios, deposit insurance) to satisfy "more like." CON's strategy of extracting concessions on specific tools (liquidity floor, no gates, no deposit insurance) and then relabeling whatever remained as "custody/trust law" was rhetorically sharp and forced useful clarifications, but it increasingly looked like a semantic maneuver: CON kept adopting substantively the same safeguards PRO proposed while disputing only the name. PRO's Pressure Question 2 was the pivotal exchange—it extracted CON's explicit concession that an enforceable, stress-calibrated liquidity requirement is necessary, and PRO's closing correctly leveraged that concession as evidence the dispute was over labels, not substance. CON's closing tried to hold the "trust law, not bank law" line but never explained why a forward-looking, stress-calibrated liquidity coverage requirement is meaningfully different from classic fund-style liquidity regulation. CON also suffered a real execution cost: its opening was clipped for exceeding the word limit, cutting off its concluding thought on the "third box" framing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Pressure Question 2 ("would you require enforceable liquidity standards rather than merely disclose the problem?") and CON's resulting concession ("Yes, I'd support an enforceable minimum liquid-reserve requirement"), which PRO then used in closing as the decisive admission that substantive fund-like regulation, not mere disclosure, was needed.</best_rebuttal>
